ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Usain is walking for exercise by zigzagging across a $100$-meter by $30$-meter rectangular field, beginning at point $A$ and ending on the segment $\overline{BC}$. He wants to increase the distance walked by zigzagging as shown in the figure below $(APQRS)$. What angle $\theta=\angle PAB=\angle QPC=\angle RQB=\cdots$ will produce in a length that is $120$ meters? (Do not assume the zigzag path has exactly four segments as shown; there could be more or fewer.)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a rectangular field, with A at the lower left corner, B at the lower right corner, C at the upper right corner, and D at the upper left corner. The broken-line path starts from A, passes through P, Q, R in order, and finally reaches S on the right boundary BC. Each segment of the broken line advances slanting to the right, and the angle it makes with the horizontal side AB or DC is labeled as \theta. Reasoning: The horizontal width of the field is 100 meters, and Usain's required total walking length is 120 meters. No matter how many segments the broken line has, as long as each segment goes to the right and makes the same angle \theta with the horizontal line, the horizontal projection of each segment equals the length of that segment multiplied by \cos\theta. Adding all the broken-line segments together, the total horizontal displacement is the horizontal projection of the total length, namely 120\cos\theta. Because the path starts from A on the left side and ends on the right boundary BC, the total horizontal displacement must equal the rectangle width 100 meters. Therefore 120\cos\theta=100, giving \cos\theta=\frac{5}{6}, so \theta=\arccos\frac{5}{6}.

method.method_draft: Use horizontal projection of the entire zigzag path. From the image, identify the rectangle with A at the lower left, B at the lower right, C at the upper right, D at the upper left, and the zigzag segments all slanting to the right at the same angle θ with the horizontal sides AB or DC. From the text, take the field width as 100 meters and the total desired walked length as 120 meters, with the path starting at A and ending somewhere on BC. Since every segment advances rightward and makes angle θ with the horizontal, the horizontal component of each segment is its length times cos θ. Summing over however many segments occur, total horizontal advance is 120 cos θ. This must equal the rectangle width 100, so cos θ = 100/120 = 5/6, giving θ = arccos(5/6).
